headline: Mexico Brings Bison Back to Desert After 200 Years
meta_description: Forty-eight bison have been reintroduced to Mexico's Cuatrociénegas biosphere reserve, restoring a keystone species absent for two centuries and revitalizing f…
summary_short: After 200 years, bison are roaming Mexico's Chihuahua Desert again. Forty-eight animals were released into a protected reserve to restore balance to this unique ecosyste…
body:
Forty-eight bison arrived at El Santuario Wildlife Reserve in Cuatrociénegas, Mexico, last year, marking a triumphant return for a species that had vanished from the region two centuries earlier. The reintroduction represents far more than nostalgia—it's a calculated ecological restoration project grounded in how these thousand-pound animals naturally regenerate grasslands and arid ecosystems. Their hooves break compacted soil, allowing water and seeds to penetrate deeper. Their coats disperse seeds across vast distances. Their dung fertilizes depleted earth. As Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas stated when the transfer was completed: "Today we are not just recovering a species: we are recovering balance, memory, and hope for a sustainable future."

The 324-square-mile Cuatrociénegas landscape is a jewel of Mexico's Coahuila state—a federally protected biosphere reserve defined by deep pools, gypsum crystal dunes, and rich plant life that thrives improbably within the surrounding desert. For millennia, bison acted as ecosystem anchors here before vanishing. Their absence left the sensitive arid grasslands diminished. The reintroduction taps into a growing global movement: from Great Britain to the American West, bison are being deployed as tools for natural ecosystem management.

Yet challenges remain. Kept within roughly 10,000 acres, overpopulation poses a real concern, especially without the Mexican wolves that once preyed on bison herds. Conflicts with local cattle ranchers operating nearby are possible. Gerardo Ruiz Smith, director of Fundación Pro Cuatrociénegas, believes sustainable bison management models from the United States and Canada can guide Mexico's path forward—potentially creating economic benefits for rural communities while allowing the landscape to flourish once more.
quick_facts: 48 bison reintroduced to El Santuario Wildlife Reserve in Coahuila, Mexico
200-year absence after bison vanished from Chihuahua Desert
324 square-mile Cuatrociénegas biosphere reserve with unique pools and dunes
Bison hooves break soil to increase water retention and seed germination
Mexican wolves, natural predators, are mostly extinct from the region
